units:
C O R E L E A D E R S H I P S K I L L S
Quick check 2
L E A D E R S H I P F O R S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y 25
A leader convenes competitors, farmers and a local NGO to fix a shared water shortage that no single firm can 
solve. Which systems-leadership capability is most at work?
A A. Seeing the larger system
B B. Delegating tasks downward
C C. Cost cutting
D D. Compliance reporting
Think, vote, then discuss. (Answer in speaker notes.)

C O R E L E A D E R S H I P S K I L L S
Quick check 2: answer
L E A D E R S H I P F O R S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y 26
Answer: A. Seeing the larger system
No firm can solve a shared water problem alone. By bringing the actors together, the leader helps them see the whole 
system, reflect on each other's views and start to co-create options. This is also an example of working at the 
ecosystem level.

S E C T I O N 3
Leading in Practice
Leaders in action: three cases, the roles leaders play and what this means for engineers.
27

L E A D I N G I N P R A C T I C E
Case: Patagonia and a founder's radical choice
L E A D E R S H I P F O R S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y 28
V A L U E S - L E D O W N E R S H I P
■ Sept 2022: founder Yvon Chouinard and family transferred ownership of 
Patagonia to a trust and a non-profit.
■ Stated aim: profits not reinvested in the business go to fight the climate 
crisis and protect nature.
■ The move came after decades of environmental activism and product￾stewardship messages such as encouraging repair.
■ Honest critique: the model works because of a founder with unique control; 
most listed firms cannot copy it, and the brand still sells new products.
L E S S O N F O R C H A N G E L E A D E R S
A leader's values were encoded in 
ownership and governance, not only 
in slogans. That makes the 
commitment harder to reverse, but 
the approach is hard to replicate in 
public companies.

L E A D I N G I N P R A C T I C E
Case: Orsted's strategic transformation
L E A D E R S H I P F O R S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y 29
L E A D I N G A B U S I N E S S T H R O U G H A P I V O T
■ Started as the Danish fossil-based energy company DONG Energy, with oil, 
gas and coal in the mix.
■ Leadership made a deliberate shift: sold the oil and gas business, moved 
toward offshore wind and later renamed itself Orsted.
■ Backed the strategy with long-term investment and a coal-exit plan.
■ Honest critique: recent years brought cost pressures, project write-downs 
and supply-chain problems for offshore wind. Check the latest company 
reports.
L E S S O N F O R C H A N G E L E A D E R S
Bold strategic leadership can reshape 
a company, but a transformation 
carries real financial and execution 
risk. Leaders must keep 
communicating honestly when 
results wobble.

L E A D I N G I N P R A C T I C E
Case: Mahindra and the internal carbon price
L E A D E R S H I P F O R S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y 30
I N D I A N C O R P O R A T E L E A D E R S H I P
■ 2016: Mahindra & Mahindra announced an internal carbon price, reported 
as the first Indian company to do so.
■ The Group later committed to become carbon neutral by 2040.
■ Reported milestones include a plant described as India's first carbon-neutral 
facility.
■ Internal pricing turns climate risk into a number that managers can use in 
investment decisions.
■ Verify the price level, scope and current status in Mahindra's own reports.
L E S S O N F O R C H A N G E L E A D E R S
Leaders can build tools into capital 
allocation, so sustainability appears 
in ordinary decisions. Be precise 
about claims such as "carbon 
neutral": ask about scope and 
offsets.

L E A D I N G I N P R A C T I C E
Four roles a sustainability leader plays
L E A D E R S H I P F O R S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y 31
Visionary
Paints a future worth 
working toward.
Convener
Brings the right people 
and rivals to one table.
Translator
Connects science, 
finance and operations 
languages.
Challenger
Questions comfortable 
assumptions and holds 
others to account.

L E A D I N G I N P R A C T I C E
Leading from where you are: engineers and technologists
L E A D E R S H I P F O R S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y 32
■ Software and data: measure the energy and carbon of 
your systems; design for efficiency and, where possible, 
carbon-aware scheduling.
■ Product decisions: engineers shape repairability, materials 
and energy use long before a manager sees the design.
■ Speak up early: raise sustainability trade-offs at design 
review, not after launch.
■ Build allies: a small group with a prototype often beats a 
policy memo.
■ Be accurate: honest numbers and clear assumptions are 
your credibility.
F O R Y O U
Leadership is a habit built early: 
take one small, visible project and 
lead it end to end.

L E A D I N G I N P R A C T I C E
When sustainability collides with short-term profit
L E A D E R S H I P F O R S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y 33
Weak responses
■ Quietly drop the goal
■ Blame the market
■ Protect the quarter and promise "later"
■ Hide the trade-off from staff
Strong responses
■ Name the trade-off and the owner
■ Reframe: cost of inaction, risk, option value
■ Phase the commitment with clear gates
■ Explain the decision openly to stakeholders

L E A D I N G I N P R A C T I C E
Governance: where leadership becomes accountable
L E A D E R S H I P F O R S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y 34
■ Board oversight: a named committee reviews climate and sustainability risk and performance.
■ Executive accountability: targets in senior scorecards, with pay linked where it is meaningful.
■ Clear roles: who owns each target, who can say no, who escalates.
■ Transparent reporting: publish progress and misses using accepted standards.
■ Why it matters: governance outlasts any one leader; it is what protects commitments after 
leadership turns over.

L E A D I N G I N P R A C T I C E
Worked example: a 360-degree assessment
L E A D E R S H I P F O R S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y 35
PROBLEM A sustainability lead rates herself and is rated by colleagues on five competencies (1-5): Systems thinking 4.2 vs 3.4, 
Anticipatory 3.8 vs 3.6, Normative 4.5 vs 4.1, Strategic 3.9 vs 3.2, Interpersonal 4.0 vs 3.0 (self vs others).
1. Gaps (self - others): 0.8, 0.2, 0.4, 0.7, 1.0
2. Self mean = (4.2 + 3.8 + 4.5 + 3.9 + 4.0) / 5 = 20.4 / 5 = 4.08
3. Others' mean = (3.4 + 3.6 + 4.1 + 3.2 + 3.0) / 5 = 17.3 / 5 = 3.46
4. Average gap = 4.08 - 3.46 = 0.62 (check: 3.1 / 5 = 0.62)
5. Largest gap and lowest rating by others: Interpersonal (1.0, 3.0). Next: Systems thinking (0.8) and Strategic (0.7).
6. Action: invest in listening and stakeholder engagement first, with a mentor and a cross-functional project.
Self-ratings run higher than others' ratings. The biggest gap, not the highest score, tells you where to develop.

L E A D I N G I N P R A C T I C E
Discussion: leading a campus initiative
L E A D E R S H I P F O R S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y 36
Scenario: you are a final-year student chairing a new campus sustainability council. You have no budget, little authority 
and sceptical wardens.
1 Is your challenge technical or adaptive? Why?
2 Which three stakeholders do you approach first, and with what message?
3 What quick win and what pilot would you choose?
4 Which of your own skills needs the most development?

S E C T I O N 4
Developing Leaders
Leaders are made, not only born. Organisations and individuals can build the skills 
deliberately.
37

D E V E L O P I N G L E A D E R S
How leaders learn
L E A D E R S H I P F O R S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y 38
■ Experience: stretch assignments, leading real projects with real stakes.
■ Relationships: mentors, peers and coaches; feedback from people who disagree.
■ Education: courses and reading give frameworks, but only help when applied.
■ Reflection: regular review of what worked, what failed and why.
■ Rule of thumb: the popular "70-20-10" split (experience, others, courses) is a rough guide, not 
an evidence-based formula.

D E V E L O P I N G L E A D E R S
Development pathways
L E A D E R S H I P F O R S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y 39
Method What it builds Example
Action-learning projects Strategic and systems skills Cross-functional team cuts site waste; reports to 
management
Job rotation Understanding of silos and trade-offs Operations engineer spends 6 months in procurement
Mentoring and coaching Self-awareness, judgment Senior leader mentors a young sustainability lead
Peer networks Resilience and shared learning Cross-company sustainability roundtable
360 feedback and reflection Awareness of blind spots Annual 360 with a development plan

D E V E L O P I N G L E A D E R S
Building a leadership pipeline
L E A D E R S H I P F O R S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y 40
■ Identify early: look for people who already convene, question and deliver across boundaries.
■ Include the frontline: leaders emerge in plants, labs and offices, not only at headquarters.
■ Diversity: varied backgrounds and perspectives improve problem-solving and legitimacy.
■ Reward the behaviour: promotion criteria should recognise sustainability leadership.
■ Make time: development fails when it is added to a full workload with no support.

D E V E L O P I N G L E A D E R S
Measuring leadership impact
L E A D E R S H I P F O R S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y 41
Level Indicators Source
Behaviour Frequency of leaders raising sustainability in decisions; 360 scores Surveys, observation
Team outcomes Participation, ideas implemented, trust and credibility scores Pulse survey, platform data
Organisational results Targets met, emissions, resource use, safety, retention Operational data
Ecosystem Supplier engagement, partnerships formed, policy contribution Programme records
Leadership effects are hard to isolate. Triangulate several measures and avoid over-claiming.

D E V E L O P I N G L E A D E R S
Leadership derailers and remedies
L E A D E R S H I P F O R S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y 42
Derailers
■ The heroic leader who does everything
■ Greenwash: words without action
■ Burnout from over-commitment
■ Ignoring those who disagree
Remedies
■ Share ownership; build a team and successors
■ Align claims with evidence and report misses
■ Set limits, delegate, build support
■ Seek dissent and test your assumptions

D E V E L O P I N G L E A D E R S
Critique: the limits of leadership-centred thinking
L E A D E R S H I P F O R S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y 43
■ Heroic leader myth: success depends on structures, incentives and collective action, not only 
on individuals.
■ Context constrains: shareholder pressure, regulation and markets limit what a leader can do, 
as the BP and Unilever examples show.
■ Survivorship bias: we study successful leaders and overlook those who tried the same and 
failed.
■ Power and fairness: leadership talk can ignore who gains and who loses from a transition.
■ Evidence: much of the sustainability leadership literature is conceptual or case-based; causal 
evidence is limited.

D E V E L O P I N G L E A D E R S
Your personal leadership plan
L E A D E R S H I P F O R S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y 44
Horizon Action Evidence of progress
Next 30 days Choose one real issue; map stakeholders; speak to three people 
who disagree
Stakeholder map; notes from 
conversations
Next 90 days Run a small pilot with measurable results; ask for 360 feedback Pilot data; feedback summary
Next 12 months Lead a project end to end; find a mentor; build a peer network Delivered result; named mentor
Beyond Take on larger, cross-boundary challenges; develop others Successors; wider partnerships

D E V E L O P I N G L E A D E R S
Key takeaways
L E A D E R S H I P F O R S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y 45
1 Sustainability leadership is an activity anyone can exercise, not a job title.
2 Tell technical from adaptive challenges; most hard problems are adaptive.
3 Core skills: systems and long-term thinking, influence, negotiation, ethical judgment.
4 Tools such as an internal carbon price make hidden costs visible in decisions.
5 Cases show both what leaders can change and the limits they face.
6 Develop leaders through projects, feedback and reflection, and be critical of the heroic-leader 
story.

Collaboration and Partnerships
Working with stakeholders to achieve shared sustainability goals

Learning outcomes
C O L L A B O R A T I O N A N D P A R T N E R S H I P S 2
■ Explain why sustainability goals require collaboration, and the main partnership types.
■ Map stakeholders using salience and the IAP2 engagement spectrum.
■ Design a partnership: partner choice, governance, trust and collective impact.
■ Quantify a shared-cost allocation, a stakeholder score and a partnership benefit-cost ratio.
■ Critique cases and the limits of partnerships, including power and accountability.

S E C T I O N 1
Why Collaborate
Climate, water, plastics and poverty are shared problems. No single firm, government or 
NGO can solve them alone.
4

W H Y C O L L A B O R A T E
Why no one acts alone
C O L L A B O R A T I O N A N D P A R T N E R S H I P S 5
■ Shared problems: emissions, water stress and waste cross 
company, sector and national boundaries.
■ Complementary strengths: firms bring capital and scale, 
governments bring rules and legitimacy, NGOs and 
communities bring local knowledge.
■ Efficiency: sharing infrastructure, data and learning lowers 
cost for each party.
■ Legitimacy: solutions designed with those affected are 
more likely to be accepted.
■ Global framing: SDG 17 calls for partnerships to deliver the 
other goals.
K E Y I D E A
Collaboration is not charity or 
public relations. It is often the 
only way to reach goals that sit 
outside one organisation's 
control.

W H Y C O L L A B O R A T E
Shareholder view vs. stakeholder view
C O L L A B O R A T I O N A N D P A R T N E R S H I P S 6
Shareholder primacy
■ Firm exists to maximise owner returns
■ Other groups matter only as means
■ Short-term financial focus
■ Collaboration seen as cost or risk
Stakeholder approach (Freeman, 1984)
■ Firm creates value for many groups
■ Those affected by or affecting the firm count
■ Long-term, relationship-based
■ Collaboration seen as a source of resilience

W H Y C O L L A B O R A T E
A spectrum of working together
C O L L A B O R A T I O N A N D P A R T N E R S H I P S 7
Inform
Share information and 
updates.
Coordinate
Align schedules and avoid 
duplication.
Cooperate
Support each other's separate 
projects.
Collaborate
Plan and deliver jointly 
toward shared goals.
Integrate
Merge resources, governance 
or operations.
A teaching model. More integration is not always better: choose the level that fits the goal and the trust available.

W H Y C O L L A B O R A T E
Types of partnership in sustainability
C O L L A B O R A T I O N A N D P A R T N E R S H I P S 8
Type What it looks like Main risk
Supplier collaboration Joint emissions or safety programmes with suppliers Power imbalance; cost shifted to small 
suppliers
Business and NGO Standards, restoration or community projects Reputation risk; greenwashing perception
Public-private Infrastructure, waste, water or energy projects Unclear risk sharing; slow procurement
Industry alliances Shared targets, pacts and standards Lowest common denominator; free riders
Community partnerships Benefit sharing and local co-management Tokenism; unequal voice
Academia-industry Joint research, pilots and training Different timelines and incentives

W H Y C O L L A B O R A T E
Benefits and costs of collaboration
C O L L A B O R A T I O N A N D P A R T N E R S H I P S 9
Benefits
■ Access to resources, skills and data
■ Shared cost and risk
■ Legitimacy and social licence
■ Learning and faster scale
Costs and risks
■ Time and coordination effort
■ Loss of control and flexibility
■ Free riders and unequal contributions
■ Shared reputation damage if one partner fails

W H Y C O L L A B O R A T E
Worked example: sharing a treatment plant
C O L L A B O R A T I O N A N D P A R T N E R S H I P S 10
PROBLEM Three firms need effluent treatment. Flows: A 200, B 300, C 500 m3/day. Standalone capex: A Rs 4 crore, B Rs 5 crore, C Rs 7 
crore (total Rs 16 crore). A shared plant costs Rs 11 crore (illustrative).
1. Total saving = 16 - 11 = Rs 5 crore (31.25% of standalone cost).
2. Rule 1, split by flow (20%, 30%, 50%): A Rs 2.2, B Rs 3.3, C Rs 5.5 crore.
3. Savings: A 4 - 2.2 = 1.8 (45%); B 5 - 3.3 = 1.7 (34%); C 7 - 5.5 = 1.5 (21.4%). All are better off than going alone.
4. Rule 2, equal percentage saving: each pays 68.75% of standalone: A 2.75, B 3.44, C 4.81 crore (sum 11.0).
5. Which is fair? Rule 1 favours small users; Rule 2 shares gains equally. The choice is a negotiation, not a formula.
6. Stability check: no firm should be able to do better by leaving. Here, each pays less than standalone cost.
The partnership works only if every party gains. How the gain is shared is where collaboration is won or lost.

W H Y C O L L A B O R A T E
Quick check 1
C O L L A B O R A T I O N A N D P A R T N E R S H I P S 11
A local fishing community has a legitimate claim and an urgent grievance against a port expansion, but little 
formal power. In Mitchell, Agle and Wood's salience model, this is a:
A A. Dormant stakeholder
B B. Dependent stakeholder
C C. Definitive stakeholder
D D. Discretionary stakeholder
Think, vote, then discuss. (Answer in speaker notes.)

W H Y C O L L A B O R A T E
Quick check 1: answer
C O L L A B O R A T I O N A N D P A R T N E R S H I P S 12
Answer: B. Dependent stakeholder
Mitchell, Agle and Wood classify stakeholders by three attributes: power, legitimacy and urgency. Legitimacy and 
urgency without power is dependent: the group needs others (regulators, NGOs, the firm) to take up its claim. Good 
practice is to engage such groups directly rather than wait for them to gain power.

S E C T I O N 2
Mapping and Engaging
Before you partner, know who is affected, who can affect you, and how deeply each 
should be involved.
13

M A P P I N G A N D E N G A G I N G
Who are your stakeholders?
C O L L A B O R A T I O N A N D P A R T N E R S H I P S 14
Internal
Employees, managers, 
owners, unions, students 
and staff.
Value chain
Suppliers, distributors, 
customers, contractors.
External
Regulators, investors, 
communities, NGOs, 
media, peers.
Silent
Nature and future 
generations: no voice, so 
someone must speak for 
them.

M A P P I N G A N D E N G A G I N G
Stakeholder salience: power, legitimacy, urgency
C O L L A B O R A T I O N A N D P A R T N E R S H I P S 15
Class Attributes present Engagement implication
Dormant Power only Monitor; may activate later
Discretionary Legitimacy only Keep informed; good for voluntary projects
Demanding Urgency only Listen; avoid over-reacting
Dominant Power + legitimacy Engage regularly; they expect influence
Dangerous Power + urgency Manage carefully; risk of coercion
Dependent Legitimacy + urgency Give voice; ensure their claim is heard
Definitive All three Top priority; engage immediately
Source: Mitchell, Agle and Wood (1997). Attributes change over time, so revisit the map regularly.

M A P P I N G A N D E N G A G I N G
The IAP2 spectrum of public participation
C O L L A B O R A T I O N A N D P A R T N E R S H I P S 16
Inform
Provide balanced 
information.
Consult
Gather feedback on 
options or decisions.
Involve
Work directly so 
concerns are 
understood and 
considered.
Collaborate
Partner in 
developing 
alternatives and 
choosing a solution.
Empower
Place final decision 
in the hands of the 
stakeholders.

M A P P I N G A N D E N G A G I N G
Activity: choose the engagement level
C O L L A B O R A T I O N A N D P A R T N E R S H I P S 17
Place each situation at the engagement level that best describes it. Discuss in pairs for 3 minutes.
Inform / Consult
One-way or limited feedback
Involve
Concerns shape the options
Collaborate / Empower
Joint or stakeholder decision
1. "A firm posts notice of a plant expansion with a comment form."
2. "Workshops with residents shape three design options; the firm decides."
3. "A village committee and the firm jointly choose the waste-site location."
4. "A company sends a newsletter about its new recycling scheme."
5. "A community trust decides how benefit-sharing funds are spent."
6. "A survey asks suppliers which support they would value."

M A P P I N G A N D E N G A G I N G
Engagement methods
C O L L A B O R A T I O N A N D P A R T N E R S H I P S 18
Surveys
Wide reach; limited depth.
Workshops
Dialogue and co-design in small 
groups.
Advisory panels
Standing groups for regular advice.
Site visits
See the issue first hand.
Grievance channels
A safe, trusted way to raise 
complaints.
Joint projects
Learn by working together.

M A P P I N G A N D E N G A G I N G
Positions vs. interests
C O L L A B O R A T I O N A N D P A R T N E R S H I P S 19
Positions (what they say)
■ "No expansion near our village."
■ "We cannot raise prices."
■ "The regulator must act."
■ Rigid; leads to win-lose bargaining
Interests (what they need)
■ Safe water, livelihood, health, respect
■ Margin, volume, predictable costs
■ Fair rules, evidence, accountability
■ Flexible; opens room for joint options

M A P P I N G A N D E N G A G I N G
Worked example: scoring stakeholder salience
C O L L A B O R A T I O N A N D P A R T N E R S H I P S 20
PROBLEM Score each group 1 to 5 on power (P), legitimacy (L) and urgency (U); salience = P + L + U (a simple screening score, 
illustrative).
1. Regulators: P 5, L 5, U 3, score = 13
2. Local community: P 2, L 5, U 5, score = 12
3. Investors: P 4, L 4, U 2, score = 10
4. Employees: P 3, L 4, U 3, score = 10
5. Suppliers: P 3, L 3, U 2, score = 8
6. Insight: the community ranks second despite low power. A power-only view would put it last and miss the biggest social 
licence risk.
Use scores to start a conversation, not to end one. Always check with the groups themselves.

M A P P I N G A N D E N G A G I N G
Communities and free, prior and informed consent
C O L L A B O R A T I O N A N D P A R T N E R S H I P S 21
■ FPIC: free, prior and informed consent is a principle in the 
UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples and in 
many corporate and finance standards.
■ Free: no coercion or manipulation.
■ Prior: before decisions and in good time.
■ Informed: full, understandable information, including risks.
■ Consent: the community may say no. Consultation without 
the option to refuse is not consent.
W H Y I T M A T T E R S
Projects that ignore local rights 
face delays, litigation and loss of 
social licence, and may cause real 
harm. Treat it as a standard of 
respect, not paperwork.

M A P P I N G A N D E N G A G I N G
Case: Kalundborg Symbiosis
C O L L A B O R A T I O N A N D P A R T N E R S H I P S 22
I N D U S T R I A L C O L L A B O R A T I O N O V E R D E C A D E S
■ Denmark: a cluster of companies and the municipality exchange waste heat, 
water, gypsum, steam and by-products.
■ Exchanges grew step by step from the 1960s and 1970s, mostly on bilateral 
commercial deals.
■ Each link is justified by cost savings and resource use; the environmental 
gain follows.
■ Honest critique: it grew from specific local conditions and geography, so it is 
hard to copy elsewhere.
■ Verify current members and quantities on the Symbiosis website.
L E S S O N F O R C H A N G E L E A D E R S
Trust built through small commercial 
exchanges can grow into a system. 
Start with deals that make economic 
sense for both parties; do not wait 
for a grand plan.

M A P P I N G A N D E N G A G I N G
Quick check 2
C O L L A B O R A T I O N A N D P A R T N E R S H I P S 23
A company forms a joint committee with community representatives to develop alternatives and choose the 
preferred solution together. On the IAP2 spectrum this is mainly:
A A. Inform
B B. Consult
C C. Collaborate
D D. Empower
Think, vote, then discuss. (Answer in speaker notes.)

M A P P I N G A N D E N G A G I N G
Quick check 2: answer
C O L L A B O R A T I O N A N D P A R T N E R S H I P S 24
Answer: C. Collaborate
IAP2 defines Collaborate as partnering with the public in each aspect of the decision, including developing alternatives 
and identifying the preferred solution. Empower goes further by placing the final decision in the stakeholders' hands.

S E C T I O N 3
Building Partnerships
How to find the right partners, set up good governance, build trust and deliver collective 
impact.
25

B U I L D I N G P A R T N E R S H I P S
The partnership lifecycle
C O L L A B O R A T I O N A N D P A R T N E R S H I P S 26
Scope
Agree the problem, goals and who 
needs to be at the table.
Build
Select partners, define roles, 
governance and resources.
Manage
Deliver, communicate, resolve 
conflicts, measure.
Renew or exit
Review results; expand, adapt or end 
responsibly.
Plan the exit at the start. A partnership with no end or review point tends to drift.

B U I L D I N G P A R T N E R S H I P S
Choosing partners: what to look for
C O L L A B O R A T I O N A N D P A R T N E R S H I P S 27
Criterion Questions to ask Red flag
Shared goal Do we want the same outcome, even for different reasons? Hidden agenda; partner wants only publicity
Complementary assets What does each side bring that the other lacks? Duplicated strengths; unclear contribution
Credibility Track record, transparency, reputation? History of broken promises
Capacity Staff, time and money to follow through? Over-committed; one champion only
Values and ethics Compatible standards on rights, anti-corruption, 
environment? Conflicts on core principles

B U I L D I N G P A R T N E R S H I P S
Collective impact: five conditions (Kania and Kramer)
C O L L A B O R A T I O N A N D P A R T N E R S H I P S 28
Common agenda
Shared vision and 
understanding of the 
problem.
Shared 
measurement
Agreed indicators 
and data across 
partners.
Mutually 
reinforcing
Different activities 
that coordinate into 
one plan.
Continuous 
communication
Regular contact to 
build trust and 
alignment.
Backbone 
support
A dedicated team to 
coordinate the 
effort.

B U I L D I N G P A R T N E R S H I P S
Governance and agreements
C O L L A B O R A T I O N A N D P A R T N E R S H I P S 29
■ Charter or MoU: purpose, scope, roles, duration and how decisions are made.
■ Decision rules: who votes, who vetoes, how deadlock is resolved.
■ Resources: who contributes money, staff and data; how costs and benefits are shared.
■ Data and IP: what can be shared, who owns results, confidentiality.
■ Disputes and exit: a clear path for conflict and a fair way to leave.
■ Accountability: regular reporting to partners and, where relevant, the public.

B U I L D I N G P A R T N E R S H I P S
Building trust between partners

B U I L D I N G P A R T N E R S H I P S
Power imbalance in partnerships
C O L L A B O R A T I O N A N D P A R T N E R S H I P S 31
Dominated partnership
■ The large partner sets goals and terms
■ Small partners bear compliance costs
■ Voice is token; exit costs are high
■ Result: resentment, hidden non-compliance
Equitable partnership
■ Goals set jointly; small partners heard
■ Costs and support shared fairly
■ Real decision rights and fair terms
■ Result: durable commitment

B U I L D I N G P A R T N E R S H I P S
Case: India Plastics Pact
C O L L A B O R A T I O N A N D P A R T N E R S H I P S 34
I N D U S T R Y A L L I A N C E W I T H S H A R E D T A R G E T S
■ Launched in 2021 by CII and WWF India, with support from WRAP, as part 
of a global Plastics Pact network.
■ Brings together businesses, government, NGOs and others around shared 
packaging goals.
■ Typical elements: eliminating unnecessary plastic, making packaging 
reusable or recyclable, using recycled content, and reporting progress.
■ Honest critique: voluntary pacts have limited enforcement, and progress 
depends on member reporting and on collection and recycling 
infrastructure.
■ Check the Pact's latest targets and progress reports.
L E S S O N F O R C H A N G E L E A D E R S
Shared targets and common 
reporting create peer pressure. They 
do not replace regulation or the 
waste-management system that the 
targets rely on.

B U I L D I N G P A R T N E R S H I P S
Case: RSPO and the limits of multi-stakeholder standards
C O L L A B O R A T I O N A N D P A R T N E R S H I P S 35
H O N E S T C R I T I Q U E
■ The Roundtable on Sustainable Palm Oil began in 2004 with producers, 
retailers, banks and NGOs such as WWF.
■ It created certification standards for more responsible palm oil.
■ Strength: it brought rivals and critics to one table and set common criteria.
■ Criticism: some NGOs and researchers argue that certification has not 
stopped deforestation or labour abuses in all cases, and that enforcement 
and audits vary.
■ Check recent reviews and the RSPO's own reports for current evidence.
L E S S O N F O R C H A N G E L E A D E R S
A seat at the table does not 
guarantee impact. The design of 
standards, auditing and 
consequences decides whether 
collaboration changes behaviour on 
the ground.

B U I L D I N G P A R T N E R S H I P S
Worked example: benefit-cost of a partnership
C O L L A B O R A T I O N A N D P A R T N E R S H I P S 36
PROBLEM A clean-cooking programme: business Rs 2 crore, government Rs 3 crore, NGO in-kind Rs 0.5 crore. It reaches 40,000 
households, each saving Rs 3,000/yr in fuel for 5 years; discount rate 10% (illustrative).
1. Total cost = 2 + 3 + 0.5 = Rs 5.5 crore; cost per household = 5.5 crore / 40,000 = Rs 13,750
2. Annual saving = 40,000 x 3,000 = Rs 12 crore
3. Annuity factor (5 years, 10%) = 3.7908, so PV of savings = 12 x 3.7908 = Rs 45.5 crore
4. Benefit-cost ratio = 45.5 / 5.5 = 8.3; NPV = 45.5 - 5.5 = Rs 40.0 crore
5. Business share of cost = 2 / 5.5 = 36%; leverage = 5.5 / 2 = 2.75 times the business money
6. Caution: claiming 36% of the impact for 36% of the cost is crude. Report shared contribution, not exclusive credit.
Each partner's money was leveraged. The programme works only because all three contributed.

S E C T I O N 4
Making It Work
Partnerships fail more often from poor management than from bad intentions. This 
section is about keeping them effective and honest.
38

M A K I N G I T W O R K
Shared goals and shared measurement
C O L L A B O R A T I O N A N D P A R T N E R S H I P S 39
■ Specific, joint targets: what, how much, by when, owned by whom.
■ Common definitions: agree on boundaries, units and methods before collecting data.
■ Avoid double counting: when several partners claim the same result, the total is overstated.
■ Data-sharing agreements: who sees what, how it is protected.
■ Report openly: successes, misses and lessons, on a regular schedule.

M A K I N G I T W O R K
Communication and conflict resolution
C O L L A B O R A T I O N A N D P A R T N E R S H I P S 40
■ Regular rhythm: agreed meetings and a single place for decisions and records.
■ Common language: explain jargon; firms, NGOs and communities use words differently.
■ Interest-based negotiation: separate people from the problem; focus on interests; generate 
options.
■ Escalation path: agree in advance who mediates and when.
■ Listen to dissent: objections often expose real risks.

M A K I N G I T W O R K
Why partnerships fail, and safeguards
C O L L A B O R A T I O N A N D P A R T N E R S H I P S 41
Common failure modes
■ Unclear goals or roles
■ Dominant partner and silent others
■ No dedicated coordination capacity
■ Loss of the founding champion
Safeguards
■ Written charter, reviewed regularly
■ Fair decision rights and real voice
■ A funded backbone or secretariat
■ Shared ownership and succession plan

M A K I N G I T W O R K

Dimension Indicator Method

M A K I N G I T W O R K
Law and ethics: competition and greenwashing
C O L L A B O R A T I O N A N D P A R T N E R S H I P S 43
■ Competition law: rivals who coordinate on prices, output 
or sensitive commercial data may breach competition 
rules. Sustainability goals do not automatically exempt 
such agreements.
■ Safe practice: keep sustainability collaboration pre￾competitive and focused on standards, shared 
infrastructure or public goals; take legal advice.
■ Greenwashing risk: joint claims must be accurate and 
evidenced; every partner is exposed.
■ Anti-corruption: screen partners, especially in public￾private deals.
C H E C K B E F O R E Y O U S I G N
Rules differ by country and 
change over time. Treat this slide 
as a prompt to ask a lawyer, not 
as advice.

M A K I N G I T W O R K
Critique: the limits of partnerships
C O L L A B O R A T I O N A N D P A R T N E R S H I P S 44
■ Accountability gap: when many partners share responsibility, no one may be answerable for 
failure.
■ Power asymmetry: big firms and funders often set the agenda; communities and small 
suppliers have less voice.
■ Partnership as PR: a logo on a partnership page can substitute for real change.
■ Substitute for regulation: voluntary collaboration may delay binding rules that would level the 
field.
■ Evidence: much of the evidence is case-based and written by participants; independent 
evaluation is rarer.
